tagline: Four nations on two main islands
overview:
The United Kingdom is made up of four nations: England, Scotland and Wales, which together form the island of Great Britain, and Northern Ireland, which shares a smaller island with the Republic of Ireland. Altogether it is about the size of Oregon, and nowhere in it lies more than about 120 kilometers from the sea. Around 68 million people live there, most of them in England.

London, the capital, sits on the River Thames and has been a major city for nearly 2,000 years. English is the main language, and Welsh, Scottish Gaelic and Irish are spoken and taught in parts of the country. The UK is a constitutional monarchy: a king or queen serves as head of state while an elected parliament at Westminster makes the laws, and Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have an assembly for local matters. The country joined the European Union in 1973 and left in 2020.
landAndNature: The UK's landscapes change quickly for so small a country. The Scottish Highlands hold the highest ground, topped by Ben Nevis at 1,345 meters, along with deep lochs including Loch Ness. The Lake District and the Pennine ridge run through northern England, Wales rises into the peaks of Eryri, and southern England rolls in chalk downs that end in the white cliffs of Dover. The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland is a shore of about 40,000 six-sided basalt columns left by ancient lava. The Gulf Stream keeps winters mild and the weather famously changeable. Red deer, puffins, otters and red squirrels live here, and hedgerows shelter badgers and hedgehogs.
peopleAndCulture: Tea is a national habit, and roast dinners, fish and chips, curry and the full cooked breakfast all count as British food. Modern soccer was written down here, and the Premier League is watched worldwide; cricket, rugby, tennis at Wimbledon and the London Marathon fill the sporting year. The UK has shaped world culture out of all proportion to its size, from Shakespeare and Dickens to the Beatles and Harry Potter. Cities are strikingly diverse, and more than 300 languages are spoken in London alone. Older traditions run deep: bagpipes and Highland games in Scotland, Eisteddfod poetry festivals in Wales, and guardsmen in tall bearskin hats in London.
history: Stone Age builders raised Stonehenge about 4,500 years ago. Romans invaded in AD 43, followed by Anglo-Saxons and Vikings, and in 1066 the Normans conquered England. Magna Carta in 1215 limited the king's power, and parliament grew stronger after a civil war in the 1640s. England and Scotland united in 1707 and Ireland joined in 1801, though most of Ireland left in 1922. Britain built the largest empire in history, ruling roughly a quarter of the world, and British ships carried millions of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic before campaigners won abolition of the trade in 1807 and of slavery across most of the empire in 1833. Industry began here, and the empire ended after two world wars.
funFacts: The London Underground, opened in 1863, was the first underground railway anywhere in the world.
Each of the UK's four nations has its own flag, national soccer team and patron saint.
Scotland has around 790 islands, but fewer than a hundred of them have anyone living on them.
Big Ben is the name of the bell inside the tower beside parliament, not of the tower itself.
The industrial revolution began in Britain in the 1700s, powered by coal, iron and steam engines.
Britain's motorways and main roads still follow routes surveyed by Roman engineers nearly 2,000 years ago.
